I like this line of thinking. It would probably require e.g., constitutional amendments at federal and local levels. And yeah, you'd need to define how to determine when the law has been unenforced.

My approach to the problem of too many laws is that they should all automatically sunset after a maximum of e.g., 20 years. I.e., at the time of this writing, any bill that was passed before 1996 would not be considered law. If the law is something that's effective and people broadly agree on it, then it should be easy for legislatures to renew it and give it a fresh timestamp/Time To Live. Hopefully the effect would be lawmakers using the majority of their time to review existing law and force them to quickly find the boundaries of consensus/compromise (lest good laws expire and anarchic purging take hold) rather than constantly piling on and leaving it to the tax payer to pay for more and more programs and regulations so that all sides can have their cake and eat it too.

I'm going to go with no. I presume you're saying that if out of some number known instances of a law being broken, if only a small percentage were prosecuted, you'd deem the law "not enforced" and repeal it, right?

The problem is that, if you want to stick with "innocent until proven guilty," then the only confirmed instances of a law being broken are ones that are prosecuted and lead to a guilty verdict. We'd have no way of knowing if someone was guilty of committing a crime but wasn't prosecuted unless you want to presume guilt, which is a whole other argument.

Most likely not.

The only branch that has the power to 'strike down' a law (as opposed to revoking) is the Supreme Court. And the Supreme Court, with it's current approach, isn't going to strike down a law unless they have a valid Constitutional reason for doing so. A law that has been validly passed and signed into law, and which is not in violation of the Constitution, won't be struck down simply because it hasn't been used in a while. Now, if in the time that the law was passed and the present, definitions and understandings of the Constitution have changed, and it is now deemed to be in violation of the Constitution, then that would be grounds for them striking it down. But the passage of time and non-enforcement isn't a violation of the Constitution.

A law is normally only struck down based on constitutional violations (in the US). This does let some crazy laws get weeded out. A good alternative would be a mandatory expiration date on most laws excluding things like murder (so you don't see what already happens with the national budget happening in such a way where someone gets murder legalized in order to force agreement on another unrelated issue or rider). Then the law would have to be renewed say every 20 years if it's still relevant.
